# Allocated cap area measures and an oriented planar section body

The noncoincident surface-area identity and the binary thin-triangle aggregation obstruction are already in `candidate 4b6ce6cf06c8f669`. This note extends the identity to every consistent supporting allocation and to a cap law. Its new planar consequence retains orientation: the convex body formed by the cut-section normal measure fits, after translation, in two different scaled copies of the aggregate body. On a triangle this keeps the asymmetry information lost by the even shadow inequality and is sharp at 4/9. No mixed numerical payment follows.

## 1. The all-status area-measure identity

Let d>=2, let K_z be positive compact convex bodies at finitely many actual sampled bases, and let theta be a probability law of ambient cap records

    H={a.z+u.X>=c}.

Use the SAME body selectors s_H and allocated section measures as the actual stress. At a proper section the body selector is its captured bit and the section is fully allocated. At an inside supporting facet use body density alpha and section density 1-alpha. At an outside supporting facet both densities are alpha. Let T_H be total coarea, so |u|T_H is the total allocated section area. Pure-base records have u=0 and T_H=0. Assume the normal marginal identity

    int_H int_boundary s_H(w) phi(n(w)) dS(w) dtheta(H)
       = beta sum_z int_boundary(K_z) phi(n) dS       (1)

for every continuous phi on the unit sphere, where 0<beta<1.

For each fiber and cap define an effective area measure S^eff_(z,H):

* a positive-volume cap uses the usual surface-area measure of K_z intersect H;
* an empty cap or a touch of dimension below d-1 uses zero;
* an outside supporting facet F with allocated mass m=int_F alpha dS uses

      m(delta_(u/|u|)+delta_(-u/|u|)).               (2)

The last line is the surface-area measure of a suitable homothetic copy D of F inside F: take scale (m/|F|)^(1/(d-1)). For m=0 use a point. We use the ordinary lower-dimensional convention obtained by thickening a (d-1)-body: each of its two opposite normal atoms has weight |D|_(d-1). At an inside facet the effective measure is the full S_(K_z), irrespective of alpha.

Then, as finite measures on the continuous unit sphere,

    int_H sum_z S^eff_(z,H) dtheta(H)
       = beta S_B + R,
    S_B := sum_z S_(K_z),
    R := int_(u!=0) |u|T_H delta_(-u/|u|) dtheta(H). (3)

Here B is just a label for the aggregate measure until Section 2; in d>2 it must not be read as the Minkowski sum.

For a proper cap its boundary consists of the selected old boundary and a new flat face of normal -u/|u|. At an inside facet, the selected alpha and section allocation 1-alpha add to the old full facet measure. At an outside facet they yield the two atoms (2). These prove (3) record by record and then by integration using (1). Pure-base records are immediate.

The complement uses body selector 1-s_H and the same section allocation. Thus

    int_H sum_z S^eff_(z,H-complement) dtheta(H)
       = (1-beta) S_B + R^-,                         (4)

where R^- is the image of R under n -> -n. Every effective area measure has zero vector first moment, as does S_B. Consequently

    int n dR(n)=0,
    int_H T_H u dtheta(H)=0.                        (5)

This is an exact section-vector balance; no centroid or volume-martingale assertion is involved.

At an outside facet (2) retains the allocation's normal marginal only. Replacing alpha by a shorter flat body does NOT retain the allocation's tangential moments or its pointwise physical law. We use that representation only for normal area measures.

## 2. In the plane, the section measure is an actual convex body

Now assume d=2 and put

    B=sum_z K_z                                      (6)

as an ordinary Minkowski sum at the actual continuous coordinates. Planar surface-area measures add under Minkowski addition, so its surface measure is precisely S_B in (3). This remains valid for segments and points. For polygons it follows by merging edge vectors in angular order; for arbitrary convex bodies it follows by polygonal approximation and surface-measure continuity. Equivalently it is the distributional identity S_K=h_K''+h_K on the circle.

The balanced nonnegative measure R is the surface-area measure of a compact planar convex body J, unique up to translation; a pair of antipodal atoms gives a segment and R=0 gives a point. One direct construction traverses the curve whose vector increment is (-sin theta,cos theta)dR(theta). Equation (5) closes the curve. For any fixed normal, its scalar increment has one negative and then one positive sign around the circle; closure therefore keeps the whole curve in that supporting halfplane. Filling its jumps by segments gives the boundary of a convex body with the prescribed measure. This also explains the antipodal and zero cases without assuming a positive-area J.

Choose nonempty representatives D_(z,H) inside K_z for the effective measures: use the true cap if it has positive area, the shorter facet segment in (2), and a point in K_z for a zero measure. A point used for a strictly empty cap is only a zero-area bookkeeping representative and need not lie in H. For a cap law these choices may be made measurably, for example by using the projection of the origin onto each nonempty compact face to center its homothety, and a fixed point of K_z for empty cases. Cap intersections and their support functions are Borel on each status stratum. All representatives stay in the fixed compact union of the fibers.

Their Minkowski integral A is defined by

    h_A(v)=sum_z int_H h_(D_(z,H))(v) dtheta(H).      (7)

This is a support function: it is finite, continuous, positively homogeneous, and subadditive. Since h_D<=h_K pointwise and theta has mass one,

    A subset B.                                     (8)

Linearity of planar surface-area measure, first for finite sums and then by integration or the distributional support identity, gives

    S_A=beta S_B+S_J,
    A=beta B+J+q                                    (9)

for some translation q. Combining (8) with (9) and subtracting beta h_B from their support inequalities proves the oriented containment

    J+q subset (1-beta)B.                            (10)

Apply the same construction to the complementary representatives. Equation (4) gives another translation q' with

    -J+q' subset beta B.                            (11)

Both statements hold for the actual cap law; no finite sub-selection is necessary. Only the normal marginal identity (1) and consistent allocations were used. Equations (10)-(11) are stronger than the centrally symmetric shadow consequence

    J-J subset min(beta,1-beta)(B-B).                (12)

For example, (11) remembers whether the section body is reflected relative to B; the even shadow function forgets this. They imply the area bound

    |J| <= min(beta,1-beta)^2 |B|.                   (13)

No Kneser--Suss comparison is needed for this planar conclusion. In higher dimensions the full measure identity (3) still holds, but surface-area addition no longer equals Minkowski addition and the containment proof (7)-(11) does not carry over.

## 3. Sharp ordinary triangular calibration

Let T be a centered triangle. Its Minkowski asymmetry is exactly two:

    -T+q subset cT  for some q  implies c>=2,
    -T subset 2T.                                   (14)

To verify the lower bound, normalize its three facet functionals v_i by h_T(v_i)=1 and sum_i v_i=0. Each opposite vertex has v_i value -2, so h_(-T)(v_i)=2. The assumed containment gives 2+v_i.q<=c for every i; adding gives 6<=3c. The reverse inclusion follows from these same three facet inequalities.

Suppose a single triangle has a cap law satisfying (1), every positive cap representative is a translate of aT with the SAME 0<a<1, and every cap has area fraction beta=a^2. Then (7) gives A=aT up to translation, hence

    J=(a-beta)T  up to translation.

The reflected containment (11) and (14) yield

    2(a-beta)<=beta,
    beta>=4/9.                                      (15)

This is a bounded ordinary statement under the explicitly homothetic cap hypothesis, not a reduction of general caps to that hypothesis.

At the actual centroid of a triangle, take its three canonical vertex caps with equal weights 1/3. Each has a=2/3 and area fraction beta=4/9; the two incident caps cover a total 4/3 of every edge, and weighting by 1/3 gives the exact normal marginal (1). Thus

    J=(2/9)T,
    -J subset (4/9)T

is sharp. This recovers the factor two lost by using only the even shadow lower bound from `candidate c2eb139e074f5fb3`. It does not yet control which cap homotheties or mixed fiber shapes can occur at a bad minimum.

## 4. A genuine midpoint conversion and its limitation

For an actual planar family at P={-1,0,1}, compatibility gives

    K_-+K_+ subset 2K_0.

Therefore the aggregate in (6) satisfies

    B=K_-+K_0+K_+ subset 3K_0.                      (16)

Equations (10)-(11) retain this anchored geometry. In particular some translate of -J lies in 3 beta K_0, and

    |J|<=9 min(beta,1-beta)^2 |K_0|
         <=9 min(beta,1-beta)^2 M.                  (17)

The aggregate comparison constant nine relative to M cannot be decreased uniformly within this three-fiber family class. Let

    K_-=[-R,R] times [-1/R,1/R],
    K_+=[-1/R,1/R] times [-R,R],
    K_0=(K_-+K_+)/2.

These are the exact integer fibers of a convex body over [-1,1]. Here K_0 is the square of side R+1/R, B=3K_0, and

    |B|/M = 9(R+1/R)^2 / [(R+1/R)^2+8] -> 9.       (18)

This is an aggregate-geometry calibration only; no critical cap law or deepestness is asserted for it. Unlike the archived binary example, the required midpoint inclusion does bound the cross-shape contribution. The bound (17) is not a sharp mixed depth inequality and does not provide the parity factor in OC.

## 5. Precise surviving information

Before summarizing, there is a useful exactly weighted version when the SAME stress includes its full normal-localized affine base moment identities. Suppose

    int_boundary (W-beta) phi(n) omega(z) dS=0       (19)

for every continuous phi and every affine omega on the base. Take an affine omega>=0 on P, not identically zero, and define

    Omega=sum_z omega(z),
    B_omega=sum_z omega(z) K_z,
    R_omega=int_H [sum_z omega(z)|u|T_(H,z)]
                                      delta_(-u/|u|) dtheta(H).

Repeating Sections 1-2 with these nonnegative fiber coefficients gives an actual planar J_omega with S_(J_omega)=R_omega and translations satisfying

    J_omega+q subset (1-beta)B_omega,
    -J_omega+q' subset beta B_omega.                 (20)

The vector balance of R_omega is a consequence of (19), not an independently chosen cap-normal balance. The cap law and all its allocations stay unchanged.

If the ACTUAL weighted base mean

    p=(sum_z omega(z)z)/Omega

is integer, compatibility supplies B_omega subset Omega K_p. Equivalently, after normalizing lambda_z=omega(z)/Omega,

    -J_lambda+q subset beta K_p,
    J_lambda+q' subset (1-beta)K_p.                  (21)

Thus an affine reweighting whose mean is an integer does produce a section body in one actual fiber, with the same cap law. The section measure in (21) is the WEIGHTED measure R_lambda; it is not the original R and cannot be substituted for it.

On P={-1,0,1}, the condition that a nonzero affine omega have mean zero forces omega(-1)=omega(0)=omega(1). Consequently J_lambda=J/3, and (21) is exactly (16)-(17), without improving the factor three. Arbitrary nonaffine fiber weights are not furnished by the affine stress: multiplying by them requires a separate identity or transport argument. In particular (19) does not create a parity-efficient facet partition.

The full area-measure route is not merely its angular average: in two continuous dimensions it produces an oriented section body and the two translation containments (10)-(11), including supporting-facet allocations and infinite cap laws. The ordinary triangle verifies that orientation can retain the exact sharp constant under additional homothety data. Across fibers the aggregate still loses the labels; the archived binary obstruction remains decisive for unrestricted conversion to M. Equation (16) is one explicit conversion which legitimately uses an actual integer midpoint, not a general parity allocation.

The companion checker is `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_allocated_cap_area_and_planar_section_body_defect_transport.py`.
